description: BeyondCode is a team of curious minds passionate about game development, programming, space exploration, and creative problem-solving. For NASA Space Apps, we aim to transform NASA data and space-related challenges into engaging, interactive gaming experiences. We believe in combining creativity with technology to build something innovative, meaningful, and fun. We welcome collaboration, fresh ideas, and the opportunity to learn while pushing the boundaries of game design.
summary: SOL-30: GALE CRATER is an interactive, browser-based space mission engineering and operations simulator modeled after NASA’s Mars Science Laboratory (Curiosity Rover). Designed to bridge the gap between abstract aerospace theory and hands-on systems engineering, the game puts students in the role of both Payload Systems Engineer and Flight Director. Players navigate the complete lifecycle of a planetary mission across four phases: configuring rover subsystems in the Vehicle Assembly Building under strict budget and payload mass constraints; programming entry corridor angles and parachute triggers for Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL); managing 30 Sols of surface operations across Gale Crater while balancing battery state-of-charge, wheel degradation, data buffer bottlenecks, and Martian environmental hazards; and evaluating mission performance through a post-mortem engineering board review. Every design trade-off directly shapes surface survival and scientific return.
details:
WHAT IT DOES & HOW IT WORKS

SOL-30: GALE CRATER transforms complex spacecraft systems engineering into an accessible, high-stakes interactive simulation. Instead of treating rocket mass fractions, power budgets, and orbital telemetry as dry textbook equations, players experience how early engineering compromises ripple through an entire mission lifecycle:

1. Phase 0: Main Menu & Hohmann Transfer Terminal

Features an interactive orbital mechanics visualizer modeling the 560 million km Hohmann transfer arc (253 days) between Earth and Mars, complete with live one-way light-time radio delay calculations (3.1 to 13.8 minutes), a 3D MOLA Gale Crater altimetry topography viewer, and a one-click 2012 Curiosity Replica benchmark preset.

2. Phase 1: Vehicle Assembly & Subsystem Trade-Offs (VAB)

Players select an appropriation tier ($1,150M to $1,650M Flagship Cap) and assemble their rover across five interdependent categories: Launch Vehicle (Atlas V 401 vs. 541 payload fairings), Power Source (Triple-Junction Solar vs. Pu-238 MMRTG nuclear generator), Mobility (Milled Aluminum vs. Reinforced Titanium bogie wheels), Communications (Direct X-Band vs. UHF Electra MRO Orbiter Relay), and Scientific Payload (SAM Organic Lab, ChemCam LIBS Laser, CheMin XRD, Mastcam, MAHLI/APXS turret, RAD/DAN, and SHERLOC Deep-UV Raman). A live auto-scrolling SVG CAD schematic dynamically updates in real time, enforcing NASA's authentic 899.0 kg landed rover mass and 75.0 kg science payload bay limits.

3. Phase 2: Entry, Descent, and Landing ("Seven Minutes of Terror")

Due to the one-way speed-of-light communication delay, players cannot manually pilot the descent. Instead, they pre-configure entry corridor flight path angles and supersonic parachute deployment triggers. A dual-envelope telemetry simulator and zoomed Spacecraft Stage Camera (modeling 1,950°C PICA plasma bow shocks, disk-gap-band parachute inflation, heat shield separation with radar altimetry, and the 8-engine Sky Crane lowering the rover on 7.5m nylon bridles) trade landing precision against structural crash risk.

4. Phase 3: 30-Sol Surface Operations in Gale Crater

Players step into the shoes of the Surface Operations team, issuing daily command uplinks ([1] Traverse, [2] Science Payload, [3] DSN/MRO Downlink, [4] Recharge) across six geological sectors from Bradbury Landing (1.0x science multiplier) to the Mount Sharp Sulfate Unit (2.8x multiplier). A live Hazcam/Navcam surface viewer animates 6-wheel rocker-bogie suspension articulation over ventifact rocks, pulsing ChemCam LIBS laser plasma zaps, robotic arm drilling, and MRO orbital data uplinks while managing Battery State-of-Charge, Wheel Structural Integrity, and a 150 MB Onboard Flash Memory buffer against Martian dust storms and cosmic ray bit-flips.

5. Phase 4: NASA Review Board Post-Mortem

At Sol 30 (or upon mission termination), the simulator generates a comprehensive Mission Engineering Report grading the mission (S to F), calculating the Science-per-Million-Dollars Efficiency Ratio, and delivering detailed engineering feedback on hardware trade-offs.

INTENDED IMPACT & BENEFITS

Students rarely get to experience a space mission from cradle to grave. By compressing a multi-year planetary mission into a 10-minute replayable loop, SOL-30 helps learners intuitively grasp why real engineers cannot simply "put every instrument on the rover." Players immediately feel the downstream consequences of shaving wheel mass when sharp ventifacts puncture aluminium treads on Sol 14, or when high-yield SAM spectrometer runs overflow the onboard memory buffer without an orbital UHF relay.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES & ARCHITECTURE

- Frontend & State Engine: Built as a fully responsive, zero-dependency single-page application using React 18, JavaScript (ES6+), and Tailwind CSS.

- Audio Architecture: Procedural Web Audio API synthesizer providing industrial avionics sound effects and an ambient deep-space synthesizer soundtrack with a live volume control slider.

- Visuals & Telemetry: Custom dynamic SVG CAD blueprints, interactive Hohmann transfer canvas, MOLA altimetry wireframes, and live Hazcam surface rover animation loops.

- AI / Super Intelligence (SI) Disclosure: Code architecture, simulation balancing, and descriptive mission metadata were accelerated using AI/Large Language Model assistance (Google Gemini).
